Eggs of the Black-tailed gull incubated at a controlled temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] typically hatch after an incubation period of approximately 25 days [ab = approximately 25 days], a duration that aligns closely with values reported for other Larus species of comparable egg size. Newly hatched chicks emerge with a downy coat and are immediately capable of limited locomotion, characteristic of the semi-precocial developmental mode common among gulls. Upon emergence, the initial wet weight of the hatchling is approximately 66 grams [Ww0 = approximately 66 grams], though this mass declines slightly in the first day as the yolk sac is fully resorbed before the onset of exogenous feeding. The wet weight at birth stabilizes at around 48.3 grams [Wwb = around 48.3 grams] once the yolk reserves are depleted and the chick begins to receive regular provisioning from both parents. This weight loss immediately following hatching is typical for semi-precocial seabirds and reflects the metabolic cost of early activity before steady parental feeding is established.

Under the thermal conditions that characterize the active metabolic period of this species, generally around 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], the developmental trajectory of the Black-tailed gull follows a well-defined schedule. Fledging, marked by the achievement of sustained flight, occurs at roughly 30 days after hatching [tx = roughly 30 days after hatching], a relatively short nestling period compared to some larger Larus species at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. The attainment of puberty, however, is considerably delayed, with individuals reaching sexual maturity at approximately 90 days after hatching [tp = approximately 90 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This gap between fledging and reproductive competence is common among gulls, as young birds require an extended period to refine foraging skills, establish social hierarchies, and accumulate sufficient body reserves before they can successfully breed. During this sub-adult phase, birds often congregate in non-breeding flocks, ranging widely along coastal areas before returning to natal colonies. The extended post-fledging period also enables young gulls to explore foraging habitats across a broad geographic range, thereby building the navigational experience needed to locate productive feeding sites during their later breeding years.

First breeding among Black-tailed gulls typically does not occur immediately upon reaching sexual maturity. Under the same thermal regime of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], the time since birth at first brood is approximately 730 days [tR = approximately 730 days], indicating that most individuals defer reproduction for a substantial period after attaining puberty. This delayed onset of breeding is a well-documented life-history strategy in large Laridae, allowing young birds to gain experience in territory establishment and intra-specific competition. During this interval, sub-adult birds engage in courtship displays and may form pair bonds, yet successful egg-laying is rarely observed before the second or third year. The energetic demands of producing a clutch, combined with the need to secure a high-quality nesting site, likely contribute to this extended pre-reproductive interval. Field studies on nearby colonies have confirmed that few two-year-old birds successfully fledge young, and the majority of first-time breeders are at least three years old.

Adult body mass in Black-tailed gull exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, as is common among large gulls. The ultimate wet weight for females reaches approximately 522 grams [Wwi = approximately 522 grams], while males attain a larger asymptotic mass of about 591 grams [Wwi = about 591 grams]. This size difference is reflected in other morphological traits, including bill length and tarsus depth, which are consistently greater in males. The functional significance of this dimorphism has been linked to competitive interactions during the breeding season, where larger males are more successful in acquiring and defending nesting territories. Females, despite their smaller body size, invest heavily in egg production, with a single clutch of two to three eggs representing a substantial proportion of their body reserves. The mass values reported here fall within the expected range for medium-sized Larus species, though local populations along the Japanese coast may show slight variation depending on prey availability.

Longevity records for the Black-tailed gull indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 31.8 years [am = approximately 31.8 years] under the typical thermal conditions of their temperate breeding range at 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This lifespan is comparable to that of other long-lived seabirds in the Laridae family, reflecting a life-history strategy characterized by delayed maturity, low annual fecundity, and high adult survival. Breeding pairs typically produce a single clutch per year, with females laying two to three eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two to three eggs per clutch], and most pairs successfully rear at most one brood annually [F_R_i = one brood annually]. This modest reproductive output is balanced by the extended reproductive lifespan of adults, which can breed for over two decades. The combination of slow maturation and low fecundity makes the species particularly vulnerable to anthropogenic threats such as oil spills and habitat disturbance at breeding colonies, as population recovery rates are inherently slow.
